title: Many seedlings push up through the soil bent into a hook, to shield their tip

cover.alt: A cross-section of soil behind glass, with sprouting lima beans sending pale roots down and curved green shoots up.

body: Many young shoots, like these beans, don't drive up through the soil tip first. One side of the upper stem grows faster than the other, bending the top into an **apical hook**, so the sturdy curve leads the way while the delicate growing tip and seed leaves follow behind it, protected from damage. The hook holds its shape for as long as the seedling is pushing through the dark soil. Once it breaks the surface the hook is no longer needed, and light triggers it to open.

slides.alt: Lima bean shoots, bent like upside-down letter Js, rise through soil behind glass; then above ground the hooked stems lift the pale seed halves into the air and begin to unbend.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of lima beans sprouting behind glass: each shoot pushes up through the soil bent into a hook, then the hooked stems rise into the light and begin to open.

steps.label: Formation: it bends as the shoot emerges
Maintenance: it holds the bend in the soil

left.label: Tip first
left.text: The growing tip, which makes all the new stem and leaves, and the seed leaves would be pushed straight into the soil.

right.label: Hook first
right.text: The bent stem leads, and the tip and seed leaves are tucked behind it, out of harm's way.

slides.question: What makes the shoot bend into a hook?
options: One side of the stem grows faster
A fibre that pulls like a muscle
slides.explanation: Cells on one side of the upper stem expand more than on the other, and the faster side ends up on the outside of the curve. The plant hormone auxin controls this.

slides.heading: Beans lift their seed leaves
slides.text: Beans sprout ‘epigeally’: the stem below the seed leaves lengthens and pushes them above the ground, as the clip shows. In other plants the seed leaves stay buried, which is called hypogeal germination.

source.label: Abbas, Alabadí & Blázquez, Frontiers in Plant Science (2013)
